{{Short description|Straight line that only contains one real point}}

In [[complex geometry]], an '''imaginary line''' is a [[line (geometry)|straight line]] that only contains one [[real point]]. It can be proven that this point is the intersection point with the [[complex conjugate line|conjugated line]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Patterson | first = B. C.
 | authorlink=Boyd Patterson 
 | doi = 10.2307/2303867
 | journal = The American Mathematical Monthly
 | mr = 0006034
 | pages = 589–599
 | title = The inversive plane
 | volume = 48
 | year = 1941}}.</ref>

It is a special case of an [[imaginary curve]].

An imaginary line is found in the [[complex projective plane]] P<sup>2</sup>(C) where points are represented by three [[homogeneous coordinates]] <math>(x_1,\ x_2,\ x_3),\quad x_i \isin C .</math>

[[Boyd Patterson]] described the lines in this plane:<ref>Patterson 590</ref>
:The locus of points whose coordinates satisfy a homogeneous linear equation with complex coefficients
:::<math> a_1\ x_1 +\  a_2\ x_2 \ + a_3\ x_3 \ =\  0</math>
:is a straight line and the line is ''real'' or ''imaginary'' according as the coefficients of its equation are or are not proportional to three [[real number]]s.

[[Felix Klein]] described imaginary geometrical structures: "We will characterize a geometric structure as imaginary if its coordinates are not all real.:<ref>Klein 1928 p 46</ref>

According to Hatton:<ref>Hatton 1929 page 13, Definition 4</ref>
:The locus of the [[fixed point (mathematics)|double points]] (imaginary) of the overlapping [[involution (mathematics)|involution]]s in which an overlapping involution pencil (real) is cut by real transversals is a pair of imaginary straight lines.
Hatton continues,
: Hence it follows that an imaginary straight line is determined by an imaginary point, which is a double point of an involution, and a real point, the vertex of the involution pencil.
